subject: AI & Agents
title: The Confusion Matrix: A Map of Mistakes
description: A quick, practical guide to The Confusion Matrix: A Map of Mistakes.

hook.text: Your model makes mistakes. The confusion matrix tells you exactly which mistakes and how often.

buildup.text: It's a table showing true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.

discovery.text: False positives: crying wolf. False negatives: missing the wolf. Both have different costs.

twist.text: In medicine, a false negative (missed disease) is far worse than a false positive (extra test).

climax.text: The confusion matrix is the foundation for precision, recall, F1, and every evaluation metric.

punchline.text: Know your mistakes by name, and you can fix them.

quiz.question: What is a false negative in a medical screening context?
options: A sick patient incorrectly classified as healthy
A healthy patient incorrectly classified as sick

details.summary: A confusion matrix shows exactly where a classifier makes mistakes: which categories it confuses with which others. It reveals patterns of errors that a single accuracy number hides.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing which specific mistakes a model makes is more useful than knowing overall accuracy. The confusion matrix guides targeted improvements and helps assess whether errors are acceptable.
takeaways: A confusion matrix shows predicted vs actual categories in a grid
It reveals specific error patterns between category pairs
True positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives are all visible

faq.question: How do you read a confusion matrix?
faq.answer: Rows represent actual classes and columns represent predictions. Diagonal cells show correct predictions. Off-diagonal cells show specific confusions: the cell at row A, column B shows how often actual A was predicted as B.

faq.question: What can a confusion matrix tell you that accuracy cannot?
faq.answer: It shows exactly which classes the model confuses, whether errors are symmetric, and where the model is strong or weak. A model with 90% accuracy might ignore an entire minority class, which only the matrix reveals.
